lessonTitle: MHC Class I and Class II Molecules

blocks.text: A 28-year-old man develops chronic low back pain that is worse in the morning and eases with exercise. Blood typing reveals he carries HLA-B27, a variant of a single gene on chromosome 6 that is found in the great majority of people with this condition, yet most carriers never develop it. Why should one gene's variant on a presenting molecule affect disease at all?

blocks.markdown: T cells cannot see free antigen. A T cell receptor (TCR) recognises a short **peptide** displayed in the groove of a **major histocompatibility complex (MHC)** molecule on another cell. In humans the MHC genes are called **HLA** (human leucocyte antigen) genes, located together on chromosome 6. There are two main classes of presenting molecule, which differ in structure, where they are found, which peptides they carry, and which T cell they engage.

blocks.title: MHC restriction
blocks.text: A T cell recognises antigen only as a peptide bound to a self MHC molecule. CD8⁺ T cells are restricted by MHC class I; CD4⁺ T cells are restricted by MHC class II.

blocks.markdown:
**Structure.** MHC class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) is a heavy chain (α chain with domains α1, α2, α3) non-covalently associated with **β2-microglobulin**, which is encoded on a different chromosome. The peptide-binding groove is formed by α1 and α2 and is closed at both ends, so it accepts short peptides of about 8 to 10 amino acids. MHC class II (HLA-DR, -DP, -DQ) is a heterodimer of an α chain and a β chain; the groove, formed by both chains, is open at the ends and accepts longer peptides of about 13 to 25 amino acids.

**Co-receptors.** CD8 binds the non-polymorphic α3 domain of class I; CD4 binds the non-polymorphic β2 domain of class II. This is why the MHC class determines the T cell subset engaged.

rows: Nearly all nucleated cells (and platelets); not on mature red cells
Professional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells); inducible on others (e.g. by interferon-γ)
blocks.caption: Class I versus class II

blocks.markdown: **Endogenous pathway (class I).** Proteins in the cytosol, including viral proteins made in an infected cell, are degraded by the **proteasome** into peptides. The **TAP** transporter pumps peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). There, with chaperones including calnexin and tapasin, a peptide is loaded into a newly made class I molecule, which then travels through the Golgi apparatus to the cell surface for inspection by CD8⁺ T cells. A cell infected with virus therefore displays viral peptides on class I.

**Exogenous pathway (class II).** An antigen-presenting cell takes up extracellular material by phagocytosis or endocytosis into an endosome that acidifies and activates proteases, cutting the protein into peptides. Newly synthesised class II molecules in the ER carry the **invariant chain (Ii)**, which blocks the groove so that ER peptides cannot bind and directs the complex to the endosome. There Ii is cut down to the fragment **CLIP**, and the molecule **HLA-DM** exchanges CLIP for an antigenic peptide. The class II-peptide complex moves to the surface to be read by CD4⁺ T cells.

blocks.title: Where does this peptide come from?
blocks.prompt: A virus that replicates in the cytoplasm of a hepatocyte makes a nucleoprotein. A scientist detects a nine-amino-acid fragment of that protein on the hepatocyte surface. Name the MHC molecule, the pathway, the key transporter and the T cell that will respond.

steps.text: Classify the source. The protein is made inside the cell, so it is cytosolic (endogenous) antigen.
Match the molecule. Nine residues is the length that fits the closed groove of MHC class I, and hepatocytes are nucleated cells that express class I.
Trace the pathway. Proteasome degrades the protein; TAP transports peptides into the ER; they are loaded onto class I with tapasin and calnexin; the complex travels via the Golgi to the surface.
Identify the responder. CD8 binds the α3 domain of class I, so a CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cell with a matching TCR recognises the complex.

blocks.answer: MHC class I, endogenous pathway via proteasome and TAP, recognised by a CD8⁺ T cell.

blocks.markdown: **Polymorphism and disease.** HLA genes are the most polymorphic in the human genome: there are thousands of alleles in the population, and each person expresses both inherited alleles at each locus (**co-dominant expression**). Different alleles encode grooves with different shapes and charges, so each binds a different set of peptides. This is advantageous for populations, because a new pathogen is unlikely to evade every individual. But it also means that particular alleles can be associated with disease: HLA-B27 with ankylosing spondylitis, HLA-DR4 with rheumatoid arthritis, HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 with coeliac disease, HLA-B*57:01 with hypersensitivity to the drug abacavir. These are **associations**: they raise relative risk but are neither necessary nor sufficient for disease.

blocks.caption: Relative risk, used to quantify an HLA-disease association

blocks.title: Quantifying an association
blocks.prompt: In a hypothetical cohort, 30 of 600 carriers of an HLA allele develop a disease, compared with 10 of 5000 non-carriers. Calculate the relative risk and say what it shows.

steps.text: Interpret: carriers are 25 times as likely to develop the disease, but 95% of carriers (570 of 600) remain unaffected, so the allele alone is not diagnostic.

blocks.answer: RR = 25; a strong association, but not a diagnostic test.

blocks.title: Heterozygosity widens presentation
blocks.text: Because the alleles from both parents are expressed, a heterozygote can present more different peptides than a homozygote. Population diversity of HLA also explains why transplanted tissue from another person is recognised as foreign.

points: MHC class I (HLA-A, B, C with β2-microglobulin) is on nearly all nucleated cells, carries short cytosolic peptides and engages CD8⁺ T cells; class II (HLA-DR, DP, DQ) is on antigen-presenting cells, carries longer exogenous peptides and engages CD4⁺ T cells.
Class I loading uses proteasome, TAP and the ER; class II loading uses endosomal proteases, invariant chain/CLIP and HLA-DM.
HLA polymorphism shapes which peptides are presented, giving population resilience but also disease associations such as HLA-B27 with ankylosing spondylitis.

questions.stem: Which cells normally express MHC class I?

distractorRationale.a: Dendritic cells express class I, but so do other cells.
distractorRationale.b: B cells express class I, but so do other cells.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: class I is widely expressed on nucleated cells so that any infected cell can be inspected.
distractorRationale.d: Mature red cells lack nuclei and class I.

questions.explanation: MHC class I is expressed on virtually all nucleated cells because any of them may be infected and need to display viral peptides to CD8⁺ T cells. Class II is restricted largely to antigen-presenting cells.

questions.stem: A peptide of 18 amino acids is displayed to a CD4⁺ T cell by an antigen-presenting cell. Which feature best explains the peptide length?

options.text: Class II has a groove that is open at both ends
Class I has a groove that is open at both ends
Peptides are cut by the proteasome to exactly 8 residues

questions.correctOptionText: Class II has a groove that is open at both ends

distractorRationale.a: Correct: an open-ended groove allows longer peptides to hang out of the ends.
distractorRationale.b: Class I has a closed groove accepting 8 to 10 residues.
distractorRationale.c: Proteasome peptides are loaded into class I, which does not fit this scenario.
distractorRationale.d: β2-microglobulin stabilises class I and does not alter peptide length.

questions.explanation: The class II groove is open at both ends, so peptides of roughly 13 to 25 residues can bind with their ends extending out. Class I, with a closed groove, is limited to about 8 to 10 residues.

questions.stem: Which structure transports peptides from the cytosol into the endoplasmic reticulum for loading onto class I?

distractorRationale.a: Invariant chain protects the class II groove.
distractorRationale.b: HLA-DM catalyses peptide exchange on class II.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the transporter associated with antigen processing moves peptides into the ER.
distractorRationale.d: Calcineurin is a phosphatase involved in T cell signalling, not antigen processing.

questions.explanation: TAP delivers proteasome-derived peptides into the ER lumen, where they are loaded onto class I with tapasin and calnexin. Cells lacking TAP show very low surface class I.

questions.stem: What is the function of the invariant chain in the exogenous pathway?

options.text: It transports peptides across the ER membrane
It binds the class II groove in the ER, preventing premature peptide binding and directing the molecule to endosomes
It cleaves proteins in the endosome

questions.correctOptionText: It binds the class II groove in the ER, preventing premature peptide binding and directing the molecule to endosomes

distractorRationale.a: TAP does that for class I.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: Ii blocks the groove (leaving CLIP) until the molecule reaches the endosomal compartment.
distractorRationale.c: Endosomal proteases cleave antigen, not the invariant chain's function.
distractorRationale.d: CD8 binds class I, and the invariant chain is part of class II loading.

questions.explanation: The invariant chain occupies the class II groove so that ER peptides cannot load, and it directs the complex to the endosome. There it is trimmed to CLIP, which HLA-DM replaces with antigen peptide.

questions.stem: A pharmacogenomic screen finds that people carrying one specific HLA allele have a much higher risk of a serious reaction to a drug. Which explanation best fits?

options.text: The allele alters the shape of the peptide groove so that drug-modified peptides are presented to T cells
The allele prevents all antigen presentation
The allele converts class I into class II

questions.correctOptionText: The allele alters the shape of the peptide groove so that drug-modified peptides are presented to T cells

distractorRationale.a: Correct: different grooves bind different peptide repertoires, and a drug can change what is presented.
distractorRationale.b: β2-microglobulin is encoded elsewhere and is not destroyed by an HLA allele.
distractorRationale.c: Polymorphism changes which peptides are bound; it does not abolish presentation.

questions.explanation: HLA polymorphism lies mainly in the groove, determining which peptides bind. An allele such as HLA-B*57:01 can present a drug-altered peptide, triggering a T cell hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.stem: True or false: CD4 binds the α3 domain of MHC class I.
questions.explanation: CD4 binds the β2 domain of class II; CD8 binds the α3 domain of class I. This pairing explains why class II presentation engages CD4⁺ helper cells and class I presentation engages CD8⁺ cytotoxic cells.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical study, 18 of 400 carriers of allele Z and 6 of 1200 non-carriers develop a disease. Calculate the relative risk for carriers (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: Risk in carriers is 18/400 = 0.045, and risk in non-carriers is 6/1200 = 0.005. The ratio 0.045/0.005 = 9, so carriers have nine times the risk, but because most carriers remain well the allele is not diagnostic.

questions.stem: At one HLA locus a population has two alleles with frequencies 0.30 and 0.70. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what percentage of people are heterozygous at this locus?
questions.explanation: Heterozygote frequency is 2pq = 2 × 0.30 × 0.70 = 0.42, or 42%. Heterozygotes express both alleles and so can present a broader range of peptides.

questions.stem: Contrast the processing of a cytosolic viral protein and an engulfed bacterial protein, naming the MHC class, the key steps and the responding T cell in each case.
markingGuide: Viral cytosolic protein: proteasome degradation, TAP into ER, loading onto MHC class I (tapasin/calnexin), surface display, CD8⁺ T cell
Engulfed bacterial protein: endosome with acid and proteases, MHC class II with invariant chain/CLIP, exchange by HLA-DM, surface display, CD4⁺ T cell
Identifies source of antigen (endogenous versus exogenous) as determining class
questions.explanation: The origin of the protein decides the pathway: cytosolic proteins enter class I; vesicular proteins enter class II.

questions.stem: Explain why MHC polymorphism is advantageous to a population yet is associated with autoimmune disease in individuals.
markingGuide: Many alleles with different groove shapes bind different peptides
A pathogen is unlikely to evade presentation by every individual
Co-dominant expression and heterozygosity broaden presentation
Some alleles may present self peptides or cross-reactive peptides that activate autoreactive T cells
Associations raise relative risk but are not diagnostic, since most carriers remain healthy
questions.explanation: Polymorphism helps the species cope with varied pathogens; particular grooves can, however, favour presentation of peptides that trigger autoimmunity.
